questions.prompt: One Gram-Schmidt step, after some orthogonal vectors have already been accepted, does which of the following?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of an accepted vector \(u\) is the inner product of the new vector with \(u\), divided by the squared length of \(u\). Subtracting those multiples leaves a vector orthogonal to every accepted \(u\). Adding the accepted vectors builds a sum, not a remainder. Dividing by one constant rescales the new vector and does not cancel a projection. Swapping coordinates is not the projection formula.

options: Subtract from the new vector its projections onto the orthogonal vectors already accepted.
Replace the new vector by the sum of the vectors already accepted.
Divide every coordinate of the new vector by the same constant and stop.
Swap two coordinates of the new vector so that the dot product changes sign.

questions.prompt: Using the dot product, orthogonalize \((3,\ 1)\) against the already accepted vector \((1,\ 2)\). What is the first component of the result?
questions.explanation: The inner product is \(3\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 2 = 5\), and the squared length of \((1,\ 2)\) is \(1 + 4 = 5\). The coefficient is \(5/5 = 1\). The result is \((3,\ 1) - 1\cdot(1,\ 2) = (2,\ -1)\). The first component is \(2\). Reporting \(-1\) is the second component. Reporting \(1\) is the coefficient, not a component of the remainder. Reporting \(5\) is the inner product before the division.

questions.prompt: For a symmetric matrix \(Q\), the product \(x^T Q y\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) when
questions.explanation: Symmetry makes \(x^T Q y\) symmetric and bilinear. Positive definiteness makes the squared length positive for every nonzero vector, which is the remaining inner-product axiom. A negative eigenvalue makes some squared length negative, so the product is not an inner product. A singular \(Q\) gives a nonzero vector with squared length zero. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and does not replace the sign test on each of them.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   q</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
options: \(Q\) is symmetric, including when some eigenvalue is negative
\(Q\) is singular, so at least one vector has squared length zero
\(Q\) has a negative trace, regardless of its eigenvalues
\(Q\) is positive definite, so \(x^T Q x > 0\) for every \(x \ne 0\)

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that orthogonalizes a second vector against a first one. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The inner product and the squared length are taken with the vector that was kept, so that vector has to be chosen first. The coefficient is their quotient, so both numbers have to exist before the subtraction. The difference is defined by that subtraction, so it cannot be kept before the subtraction is formed. Projecting onto the original second input, instead of onto the vector already kept, is a different calculation and is not a swap of these steps.

steps: Keep the first input vector as the first orthogonal vector.
Using that orthogonal vector, compute its inner product with the next input and its own squared length.
Divide that inner product by that squared length, and subtract the resulting multiple of the orthogonal vector from the next input.
Keep that difference as the next orthogonal vector.

questions.prompt: Which of these pairs are orthogonal in the dot product?
questions.explanation:
Orthogonality is a zero dot product.
• \((1,\ -2)\cdot(4,\ 2) = 4 - 4 = 0\).
• \((2,\ 3)\cdot(3,\ -2) = 6 - 6 = 0\).
• \((1,\ 1)\cdot(2,\ -1) = 2 - 1 = 1\).
• \((0,\ 5)\cdot(3,\ 0) = 0\).
• \((2,\ 2)\cdot(1,\ 1) = 4\).
The third and fifth pairs are not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: In the dot product, the accepted vector is \((a,\ b)\) and the next input is \((c,\ d)\). The coefficient of \((a,\ b)\) that is subtracted equals
questions.explanation: The coefficient is the inner product \(ac + bd\) divided by the squared length \(a^2 + b^2\). Every declared name appears. Subtracting the inner product without the division is the mistake of treating \((a,\ b)\) as a unit vector. Adding the squared length in the numerator, as in \((ac + bd + a^2 + b^2)/(a^2 + b^2)\), mixes the coefficient with \(1\). The product \(ac + bd\) alone is the inner product, not the coefficient.

questions.prompt: A note orthogonalizes \((6,\ 4)\) against \((2,\ 0)\) in the dot product. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The accepted vector is the one already kept, \((2,\ 0)\). The inner product is \(12 + 0 = 12\), and the squared length is \(4\). The coefficient is \(3\). Subtracting does change the vector: \(3\cdot(2,\ 0) = (6,\ 0)\), and \((6,\ 4) - (6,\ 0) = (0,\ 4)\). The last step writes the original input again, which is what you get if the subtraction is skipped. The dot product of \((2,\ 0)\) with \((6,\ 4)\) is \(12\), not \(0\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="138.9"/><polygon points="235.9,138.9 229.9,142.5 229.2,137.1" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="130.9" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="118.7" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="118.7,42.3 118.3,49.3 113.4,46.9" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="126.7" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">v</text></svg>
steps: The inner product of \((6,\ 4)\) with \((2,\ 0)\) is \(12\), and the squared length of \((2,\ 0)\) is \(4\).
reasons: The subtraction was skipped: \((6,\ 4) - 3\cdot(2,\ 0)\) equals \((0,\ 4)\), not \((6,\ 4)\).
The inner product of \((6,\ 4)\) and \((2,\ 0)\) is not \(12\).

questions.prompt: Let the inner product be \(x^T Q y\) with \(Q = \mathrm{diag}(4,\ 1)\). Orthogonalize \((2,\ 5)\) against \((1,\ 0)\). What is the second component of the result?
questions.explanation: \(Q(1,\ 0) = (4,\ 0)\), so the inner product is \((2,\ 5)\cdot(4,\ 0) = 8\). The squared length of \((1,\ 0)\) is \(4\). The coefficient is \(2\). The result is \((2,\ 5) - 2\cdot(1,\ 0) = (0,\ 5)\). The second component is \(5\). Reporting \(0\) is the first component, and a zero answer is not this component. Reporting \(2\) is the coefficient. Reporting \(8\) is the inner product. The second row of \(Q\) never enters this subtraction, because the accepted vector has a zero there.

questions.prompt: If the input list is linearly dependent, Gram-Schmidt
questions.explanation: A vector in the span of those already accepted has inner products that reproduce it exactly, so the remainder is zero. A zero vector cannot be used as a later direction, and it cannot be normalized. Dependence does not create extra nonzero vectors. The inner product is unchanged by which list you feed it. The first vector of an independent prefix stays as it is. The zero appears at the dependent position.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>one arrow from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="235.9,42.3 232.1,48.2 229.1,43.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">v</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One arrow leaves the origin in the plane.
options: makes the inner product fail to be bilinear
replaces the first vector by zero and keeps the later ones
produces a zero remainder at the dependent vector, so that remainder is not a new direction
still produces one nonzero orthogonal vector per input vector

questions.prompt: Running Gram-Schmidt in the inner product \(x^T Q y\), with \(Q\) symmetric positive definite, produces vectors that satisfy
questions.explanation: The algorithm enforces orthogonality in the inner product it was given. For \(x^T Q y\) that statement is \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\). Euclidean orthogonality is the special case \(Q = I\). A positive definite \(Q\) that stretches one axis leaves the Euclidean dot product of the results nonzero in general. The products are zero, not \(1\). Nothing in the subtraction forces \(Q d_i = d_i\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a long ellipse</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An axis-aligned ellipse, longer along the first axis.
options: \(Q d_i = d_i\), so every result is an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(1\)
\(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\) for \(i \ne j\), which is \(Q\)-conjugacy
\(d_i^T d_j = 0\) for \(i \ne j\), for every positive definite \(Q\)
\(d_i^T Q d_j = 1\) for \(i \ne j\)

questions.prompt: In the dot product, the orthogonal vectors already accepted are \(u_1 = (1,\ 0,\ 0)\) and \(u_2 = (0,\ 1,\ 0)\). For the new input \((2,\ 3,\ 4)\), what is the coefficient of \(u_2\)?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of \(u_2\) is the dot product \((2,\ 3,\ 4)\cdot(0,\ 1,\ 0) = 3\), divided by \(\lVert u_2\rVert^2 = 1\), so it equals \(3\). The coefficient of \(u_1\) is \(2\), and the remainder is \((0,\ 0,\ 4)\). Reporting \(2\) uses \(u_1\). Reporting \(4\) is the third component of the remainder, not the coefficient of \(u_2\). Reporting \(1\) is the squared length of \(u_2\).

questions.prompt: After a \(Q\)-orthogonal list has been built, scaling one vector by a nonzero constant
questions.explanation: If \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\), then \((c d_i)^T Q d_j = c\cdot 0 = 0\). Conjugacy is unchanged. The exact step length along the scaled direction changes, and the displacement, length times direction, does not. Scaling does not set later coefficients to zero, and it does not alter \(Q\). A conjugate-gradient iteration still has to build its directions. It inherits the conjugacy relation, not a command to ignore previous directions.

options: preserves \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\), so the list stays \(Q\)-conjugate
destroys conjugacy, because the product scales by that constant
forces every later conjugate-gradient direction to equal the negative gradient
replaces \(Q\) by \(Q\) times that constant
